newsitem.title: MALTA: Malta's premier calls early election.
newsitem.headline: Malta's premier calls early election.

text.p: Maltese Prime Minister Edward Fenech Adami on Monday called general elections for October 26, eight months before his term runs out, because "election expectation" has gripped the country.
Fenech Adami's Nationalist Party, which seeks European Union EU membership for the Mediterranean Island, has a three-seat majority over the Labour opposition in the 65-seat parliament.

"I called on the president (Ugo Mifsud Bonnici) at noon today and exercised my constitutional duty to advise him to dissolve parliament and to call elections for October 26," the prime minister told a news conference.

Malta's Labour Party is headed by U.S.-trained economist Alfred Sant who opposes membership of the EU. He says many EU regulations are unsuited to small countries like Malta but has called for close ties with the union, including an industrial free trade zone.
Fenech Adami and his west-leaning party were elected for a five-year term in 1987, ending some 16 years of socialism under Dom Mintoff and later Karmenu Mifsud Bonnici.
He won a second term in 1992, winning by a 13,000-vote majority, a large margin in the traditionally tight elections among Malta's 275,000 voters.
He told journalists on Monday he was going to the country "happy in the knowledge that we delivered on what we promised and justified the people's confidence in us."
Fenech Adami's government started an extensive development programme with millions of dollars being spent on a telephones network, new power station, water desalination plants and airport terminal.

Foreign Minister Guido de Marco submitted Malta's application for EU membership in 1990 and the country, much of whose trade is with the EU, has since been going through an economic restructuring programme. The EU has promised membership negotiations six months after the end of the present inter-governmental conference.

Labour leader Sant has pledged to take Malta out of NATO's Partnership for Peace programme which the country joined last year, and to remove Value Added Tax which the government introduced in January 1995.
The elections, under proportional representation, will also be contested by the small Alternattiva Demokratika which won four percent of the popular vote but no parliamentary seat in the 1992 poll.

This party says it will tackle issues largely ignored by the others, such as the environment and introduction of divorce. Malta does not have divorce and both the Nationalist and Labour parties have been wary of introducing it in a deeply-Catholic nation.
